## Overview

The Cauchy distribution is the most unusual population we investigate. Unlike all the other distributions in this project, the Cauchy has no finite mean and no finite variance. This means the ordinary CLT does not apply. No matter how large the sample size gets, the sampling distribution of the mean never settles into a normal shape. This is a case where a fundamental assumption of the CLT is violated.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup

set.seed(1278)
B <- 10000
library(moments)
```

## 1. What Does the Population Look Like?

```{r}
#| label: population-plot

x <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = 1000)
plot(x, dcauchy(x, location = 0, scale = 1), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Cauchy Population (location=0, scale=1)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density")
```

The Cauchy distribution looks somewhat like a normal distribution but with much heavier tails. Extreme values occur far more frequently than a normal distribution would predict. Crucially it has no finite mean and no finite variance — these quantities do not exist for the Cauchy distribution.

**Theoretical mean:** undefined\
**Theoretical standard deviation:** undefined

## 2. My Prediction

Since the Cauchy has no finite variance the CLT does not apply. I predict that no matter how large n gets, the sampling distribution of the mean will never look approximately normal. Instead it will continue to show extreme outliers and heavy tails regardless of sample size.

## 3. Monte Carlo Simulation

```{r}
#| label: simulation

n_values <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 500, 1000)

results <- data.frame(
  n              = n_values,
  simulated_mean = NA,
  simulated_sd   = NA,
  theoretical_se = NA,
  skewness       = NA,
  kurtosis       = NA
)

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rcauchy(n, location = 0, scale = 1)))
  
  results$simulated_mean[i] <- mean(sample_means)
  results$simulated_sd[i]   <- sd(sample_means)
  results$theoretical_se[i] <- NA
  results$skewness[i]       <- skewness(sample_means)
  results$kurtosis[i]       <- kurtosis(sample_means)
}
```

## 4. Results Table

```{r}
#| label: results-table

round(results, 4)
```

## 5. Simulated vs Theoretical Standard Error

Unlike every other distribution in this project, the Cauchy has no finite variance and therefore no finite theoretical standard error. The formula SE = σ/√n cannot be applied here because σ does not exist.

Looking at the results table, the simulated standard deviation of the Cauchy sample means does not decrease as n increases the way it does for other distributions. For the Normal or Exponential, increasing n dramatically shrinks the spread of sample means — this is exactly what the SE formula predicts. For the Cauchy, the simulated SD remains large and unstable across all sample sizes because extreme outliers continue to dominate the sample mean no matter how large n gets.

This is the most important finding for the Cauchy — it is not just that the shape fails to become normal, it is that the spread itself never stabilizes. The SE formula breaks down completely here, which is a direct consequence of the infinite variance assumption being violated.

## 6. Histograms Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
#| label: histograms
#| fig-height: 14

par(mfrow = c(5, 2))

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rcauchy(n, location = 0, scale = 1)))
  
  trimmed <- sample_means[abs(sample_means) < quantile(abs(sample_means), 0.99)]
  
  hist(trimmed, breaks = 50, probability = TRUE,
       main = paste("n =", n, "(trimmed for display)"),
       xlab = "Sample Mean", col = "steelblue", border = "white")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 7. Q-Q Plots Across Sample Sizes

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
#| fig-height: 14

par(mfrow = c(5, 2))

for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {
  n <- n_values[i]
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rcauchy(n, location = 0, scale = 1)))
  
  qqnorm(sample_means, main = paste("Q-Q Plot: n =", n),
         col = "steelblue", pch = 20, cex = 0.3)
  qqline(sample_means, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 8. Why the CLT Fails for the Cauchy

```{r}
#| label: cauchy-vs-normal

set.seed(1278)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

normal_means_n1   <- replicate(B, mean(rnorm(1)))
normal_means_n100 <- replicate(B, mean(rnorm(100)))

cauchy_means_n1   <- replicate(B, mean(rcauchy(1)))
cauchy_means_n100 <- replicate(B, mean(rcauchy(100)))

boxplot(list("Normal n=1" = normal_means_n1,
             "Normal n=100" = normal_means_n100),
        main = "Normal: Mean Converges",
        col = "steelblue", outline = FALSE)

boxplot(list("Cauchy n=1" = cauchy_means_n1,
             "Cauchy n=100" = cauchy_means_n100),
        main = "Cauchy: Mean Does Not Converge",
        col = "tomato", outline = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

For the Normal distribution the spread of sample means shrinks dramatically as n increases from 1 to 100 — exactly what the SE formula predicts. For the Cauchy distribution the spread barely changes at all. This directly demonstrates that the SE formula has no meaning for the Cauchy — increasing n does not stabilize the sample mean the way it does for distributions with finite variance.

## 9. Conclusion

The Cauchy distribution is a case where the CLT fundamentally breaks down. The reason is that the CLT requires the population to have a finite variance. The Cauchy distribution violates this assumption — its tails are so heavy that variance is infinite.

**My "normal enough" standard:**

- Histogram is visually bell-shaped and symmetric
- Q-Q plot points fall close to the reference line with no systematic curves
- Skewness is between -0.5 and 0.5
- Kurtosis is close to 3

**Answer for Cauchy:** $$\boxed{\text{No value of } n \text{ works}}$$

The sampling distribution of the Cauchy mean never converges to normality. Even at n = 1000 the Q-Q plots show severe deviation from the normal line and extreme outliers persist. Furthermore the simulated SD never stabilizes as n increases — unlike every other distribution in this project where the SE formula accurately predicted the spread. This is not a failure of the simulation — it is the correct mathematical result.

## 10. What Surprised Me

The most striking result is visible in the boxplot comparison. For the Normal distribution increasing n from 1 to 100 dramatically tightens the spread of sample means — exactly what the CLT predicts. For the Cauchy the spread barely changes at all. No matter how many observations you average together, one extreme outlier can completely dominate the sample mean. This also means the SE formula is completely useless for the Cauchy — a direct and dramatic illustration of what happens when the finite variance assumption is violated. Every other distribution in this project showed accurate SE predictions even before the shape became normal. The Cauchy shows neither.
